'''''Bauhinia variegata''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[legume family]], [[Fabaceae]]. It is native to an area from China through Southeast Asia to the [[Indian subcontinent]].<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate = 23 April 2019}}</ref> Common names include '''[[orchid tree]]''' (though not belonging to the family [[Orchidaceae]]) and '''mountain ebony'''.<ref name=GRIN/>

==Description==
{{More sources|section|date=May 2025}}[[File:洋紫荊 Bauhinia variegata 20220313093543 06.jpg|thumb|x300px|left|Almost no leaves on the tree during flowering. B. purpurea and B. blakeana, which are often confused with B. variegata, are leafy during flowering.]] 
[[File:Bauhinia Variegata "Var candida" (white flowering bauhinia).jpg|thumb|left|''Bauhinia variegata'' "Var candida" (white flowering bauhinia), India]]
[[Image:Bauhinia variegata var. variegata 50D 7055.jpg|thumb|''Bauhinia variegata'' var. ''variegata'', South Africa]]

''Bauhinia variegata'' is a small to medium-sized tree growing to {{convert|15|m|ft|}} tall and {{Convert|50|cm|in|abbr=}} in [[diameter]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Bauhinia variegata |url=https://apps.worldagroforestry.org/treedb/AFTPDFS/Bauhinia_variegata.PDF |access-date=8 May 2025 |website=apps.worldagroforestry.org}}</ref> [[deciduous]] in the [[dry season]]. The [[leaf|leaves]] are {{convert|15|–|20|cm}}<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Bauhinia variegata (Orchid Tree) |url=https://www.gardenia.net/plant/bauhinia-variegata#:~:text=Prized%20for%20its%20orchid-like%20flowers,%20Bauhinia%20variegata%20(Orchid,the%20apex%20and%20base,%20and%20resembling%20butterfly%20wings. |access-date=8 May 2025 |website=Gardenia |language=en-US}}</ref> [[obcordate]] shaped, long and broad, rounded, and bilobed at the base and apex. The [[flower]]s are conspicuous, bright pink or white, {{convert|5|–|7|cm}} diameter, with five petals.<ref name=":1" /> Pollens are elongated, approximately 75 [[microns]] in length.{{Citation needed|date=May 2025}}

The fruit is a [[seedpod]] {{convert|20|–|30|cm}} long, containing 10–15 [[Seed|seeds]] each.<ref name=":0" /> The seedpod dries completely on the tree, and when mature begins to twist into a helix or corkscrew shape, (see [[#Gallery|below]]), ultimately exploding open—with a very audible "clack"—to deliver its seeds into the environs.

The anatomy of the stem was studied by taking transverse section. [[Periderm]] and cortex were seen distinctly. Secondary [[phloem]] was wide and continuous cylindrical, it consisted of thin and narrow straight rays, three or four cylinders of discontinuous masses of fibres and randomly distributed [[sieve elements]]. Secondary [[xylem]] was diffuse porous and it included vessels, fibres, xylem rays and xylem [[parenchyma]]. Xylem fibres had thick lignified walls or some had gelatinous walls. Xylem parenchyma cells were abundant in the xylem. Xylem rays were one cell wide; they were straight and consisted of radially elongated thick walled lignified walls. [[Calcium oxalate|Calcium-oxalate]] crystals are predominantly prismatic crystals and druses type. Powder microscopical examination showed presence of fibres, parenchymatous cells, periderm and [[Vessel element|vessel elements]]. Histochemical analysis of stem showed presence of [[protein]], [[tannin]], [[lignin]] and [[cellulose]].<ref>[http://www.ijpronline.com/ViewArticleDetail.aspx?ID=321 Pharmacognostical Studies of ''Bauhinia variegata'' Linn., stem. Patel L D., '''Golwala D.K.International Journal of Pharmaceutical Research''' (IJPR) (ISSN Online: 0975-2366), Surat, India. 2012: Volume 4, Issue 3, page: 127-130.]</ref>

The anatomy of the root was studied by taking transverse section. [[Secondary phloem]] and [[secondary xylem]] were seen distinctly. Secondary phloem had fairly wide rays, dense masses of phloem fibers and radial rows of phloem elements. Secondary xylem had much wider, thin-walled vessels which were either solitary or in radial multiples. The xylem fibers constituted gelatinous type and normal type. [[Calcium oxalate crystals]] were predominantly prismatic type. Powder microscopical examination showed presence of xylem parenchyma cells, xylem fibers and vessel elements.<ref>[http://www.jyoungpharm.org/article/358 Pharmacognostical studies of ''Bauhinia variegata'' root. LD Patel and '''DK Golwala''', '''Journal of Young Pharmacist''' (JoYP) (ISSN Print: 0975-483, Online: 0975-1505), Bangalore, India. 2009: Volume 1, Issue 1, page: 36-41.]</ref> As a diploid species with 28 chromosomes, sequencing of the 314MB ''B. variegata'' genome was used to demonstrate it is the paternal ancestor of the hybrid [[Bauhinia × blakeana|Hong Kong Bauhinia (''Bauhinia x blakeana'')]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mu |first1=Weixue |last2=Darian |first2=Joshua Casey |last3=Sung |first3=Wing-Kin |last4=Guo |first4=Xing |last5=Yang |first5=Tuo |last6=Tang |first6=Mandy Wai Man |last7=Chen |first7=Ziqiang |last8=Tong |first8=Steve Kwan Hok |last9=Chik |first9=Irene Wing Shan |last10=Davidson |first10=Robert L |last11=Edmunds |first11=Scott C |last12=Wei |first12=Tong |last13=Tsui |first13=Stephen Kwok-Wing |date=1 January 2025 |title=The haplotype-resolved T2T genome for Bauhinia × blakeana sheds light on the genetic basis of flower heterosis |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/gigascience/giaf044 |journal=GigaScience |volume=14 |article-number=giaf044 |doi=10.1093/gigascience/giaf044 |issn=2047-217X |pmc=12012898 |pmid=40276955}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
They are found throughout the lower [[Himalayas|Himalayan]] moist forests through [[Pakistan]], [[Nepal]], [[India]], [[Bhutan]] through [[Northeast India]] and [[Bangladesh]] into [[Indo-Burma]] and [[South Central China]]. They inhabit both [[Tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forests|moist broadleaf forests]] (including [[Rainforest|rainforests]]) and [[Tropical and subtropical dry broadleaf forests|dry broadleaf forests]] in [[Tropical climate|tropical]] and [[Humid subtropical climate|subtropical]] climates.

==In cultivation==
[[File:春色满径Scenery in Guangzhou, China - panoramio.jpg|thumb|200px|Bauhinia variegata lined street in China]]
This is a very popular [[ornamental tree]] in subtropical and tropical climates, grown for its scented flowers and also used as a food item in many South Asian cuisines. In the [[Neotropics]], it can be used to attract [[hummingbird]]s—such as [[sapphire-spangled emerald]] (''Amazilia lactea''), [[glittering-bellied emerald]] (''Chlorostilbon lucidus''), or [[white-throated hummingbird]] (''Leucochloris albicollis'')—into gardens and parks.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baza Mendonça |first1=Luciana |last2=dos Anjos |first2=Luiz |year=2005 |title=Beija-flores (Aves, Trochilidae) e seus recursos florais em uma área urbana do Sul do Brasil [Hummingbirds (Aves, Trochilidae) and their flowers in an urban area of southern Brazil]. [Portuguese with English abstract] |journal=Revista Brasileira de Zoologia |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=51–59 |doi=10.1590/S0101-81752005000100007 |url=http://www.scielo.br/pdf/rbzool/v22n1/a07v22n1.pdf |doi-access=free}}</ref> On the other hand, in some areas it has become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] and [[invasive species|invasive]].

==Uses==
Kachnar, Kovidara, Koiralo, Kanchan are local names in the Indian subcontinent for the edible [[buds]] collected from the tree; it is widely used as an ingredient in many subcontinent recipes. Traditional kachnar curry is prepared using kachnar buds, yogurt, onions and native [[spices]]. Kachnar buds are also eaten as a stir-fried vegetable and used to make [[achaar]], a pickle in many parts of the Indian sub-continent.<ref>{{cite web |title=Kachnar - a versatile plant tree |url=https://www.technologytimes.pk/2015/05/17/kachnar-a-versatile-plant-tree/ |website=Technology Times |access-date=29 March 2020 |language=English |date=17 May 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200329195105/https://www.technologytimes.pk/2015/05/17/kachnar-a-versatile-plant-tree/ |archive-date=29 March 2020}}</ref> It shows a good antioxidant and anticancer activity.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.journalejmp.com/index.php/EJMP/article/view/30214 |title=Antioxidant and Antimutagenic (Anticlastogenic) activity of alcoholic extract of Bauhinia Variegata Linn Root. '''Dharmesh K. Golwala''', Santoshkumar Vaidya, Kishore Dholwani, Darpini S. Patel and Satyajit Sahoo. '''European Journal of Medicinal Plants''' (ISSN: 2231-0894) 2020: Volume 31, Issue 2, page: 32-39. |access-date=18 July 2020 |archive-date=18 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200718181041/https://www.journalejmp.com/index.php/EJMP/article/view/30214 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Bauhinia variegata L. {{!}} Species |url=https://indiabiodiversity.org/species/show/264732 |website=India Biodiversity Portal |language=en}}</ref>

The tree is considered very sacred in [[Hinduism]], it is called ''Kovidara'' and it is symbolically depicted on the [[Dharma Dhwaj|Dharma Dhwaja]] flag.<ref>{{cite news |title=Kovidar tree, inscribed on Ram Mandir’s ‘dharm dhwaj’, was official symbol of Ayodhya kingdom |url=https://www.moneycontrol.com/religion/kovidar-tree-inscribed-on-ram-mandir-s-dharm-dhwaj-was-official-symbol-of-ayodhya-kingdom-article-13696370.html |work=Moneycontrol}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Service |first=Statesman News |date=25 November 2025 |title=Kovidara Tree: PM Modi hoists Dharma Dhwaj in Ayodhya with this plant, know its significance and medicinal value |url=https://www.thestatesman.com/lifestyle/kovidara-tree-pm-modi-hoists-dharma-dhwaj-in-ayodhya-with-this-plant-know-its-significance-and-medicinal-value-1503517127.html |access-date=25 November 2025 |website=The Statesman |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Buitenen |first1=Johannes Adrianus Bernardus |last2=Fitzgerald |first2=James L. |title=The Mahābhārata |date=1973 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=978-0-226-84664-4 |language=en |page=892 |quote=''Kovidara: bauhinia variegata''}}</ref>

In [[Nepal]], the plant is known as ''koiralo'' and the flower is known as ''koiralo ko phool'' in [[Nepali language]]. The flower and the buds are used to make Nepalese style achaar. The achar is important part of the meal served during the [[Ghode Jatra|Ghode Jatra festival]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=17 April 2015 |title=Koiralo ko Phool ko Achaar |url=https://www.thegundruk.com/koiralo-ko-phool-ko-achaar/ |access-date=9 January 2022 |website=The Nepali Food Blog {{!}} theGundruk.com |language=en-US}}</ref>
